0.title: The Secret of Peace in Every Circumstance
0.essay:
Anxiety is one of the defining struggles of our age. Many people live with a constant low hum of worry about money, health, children, work, the future or the state of the world. Others face crippling anxiety that affects their sleep, their bodies and their relationships.

A culture of discontent

At the same time, our culture constantly feeds discontent. Advertising, social media and comparison tell us that we need more, that others have it better, and that we will be happy when our circumstances change. Anxiety and discontent are close relatives. Both look at our circumstances and conclude that we cannot be at peace until something changes.

A different path

Scripture offers another way. Paul, writing from prison, said, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). And he promised that “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).

This study does not offer quick fixes. Anxiety can have many causes, some of them physical, and those who struggle deeply need patient care, sometimes including medical help. But Scripture speaks with deep comfort to anxious and discontented hearts, pointing us to a Father who knows what we need, and to a peace that circumstances cannot take away.

The chapters

The Anxious Heart; Casting Our Cares on God; Learning Contentment; The Enemies of Contentment; and Peace in the Storm. The Biblical Counseling study has a fuller chapter on caring for those with anxiety.

1.title: The Anxious Heart
1.essay:
“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on” (Matthew 6:25). Jesus spoke these words to ordinary people, many of them poor, for whom food and clothing were real concerns. He did not dismiss their needs. He pointed them to their Father.

The birds and the lilies

“Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” (Matthew 6:26). God clothes the flowers of the field more beautifully than Solomon in all his glory. If he cares for birds and grass, he will care for his children. Anxiety often forgets who our Father is.

Jesus gives several reasons not to worry, and every one rests on who God is. Life is more than food. God feeds the birds and clothes the lilies. Worry cannot add an hour to life. The Gentiles seek after these things, “and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). The cure for anxiety is not positive thinking but a deeper knowledge of the Father’s care.

Worry adds nothing

“And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” (Matthew 6:27). Worry promises control but delivers none. It borrows tomorrow’s trouble and spoils today. “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34).

Jesus’ alternative to anxiety is not passivity but priority: “But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Anxiety shrinks when our hearts are set on God’s purposes rather than our own security.

Fear not, little flock

Luke’s version ends with a tender word: “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). God is not reluctant or stingy. He delights to give his children the greatest gift of all, and if he has given us the kingdom, he will not withhold what we need. Notice too how gently Jesus speaks. Christians struggling with anxiety should not be made to feel that they are simply faithless. Rebuke without comfort only adds to the burden.

Martha and Mary

Martha welcomed Jesus into her home and “was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). She complained that her sister was not helping. Jesus answered gently: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion” (Luke 10:41–42). Mary had chosen to sit at his feet and listen. Jesus did not condemn Martha’s service, but he called her to what mattered most. Anxiety often comes from busyness that crowds out time with Christ.

Not all concern is sin

Paul spoke of “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28). Caring deeply about people and responsibilities is not sinful. Jesus himself “began to be greatly distressed and troubled” in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Scripture distinguishes responsible concern, which leads us to pray and act, from anxious worry, which assumes the worst and forgets God.

Anxiety is often a mixture: legitimate fear, because we live in a dangerous world; distorted fear, which magnifies threats beyond their reality; and unbelief, which trusts something other than God for our safety. It can also have physical contributors, such as illness, exhaustion or hormonal changes. Wise care addresses all of these, patiently.

Talking back to our fears

The psalmists were not afraid to admit their turmoil. “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation” (Psalm 42:5). The psalmist is downcast and far from home, feeling forgotten by God and mocked by enemies. Yet he speaks to his own soul, and he repeats the refrain (Psalm 42:11). He spoke honestly to God, and then he spoke truth to himself. Fighting anxiety often means talking back to our fears with the truth about God.

A young mother lies awake worrying about her children’s health, the family finances and her own inadequacy. She feels guilty for worrying, which makes her worry more. A friend sits with her, reads Matthew 6:25–34 and says, “Your Father knows. You don’t have to carry this alone.” They pray together. The worries do not vanish, but she sleeps better that night.

What are you most anxious about right now? Have you told your Father about it?

For reflection

What are the main sources of anxiety in your life right now? Which of Jesus’ reasons not to worry in Matthew 6:25–34 speaks most to you? What is the difference between responsible concern and anxious worry? How could you talk back to your fears with the truth about God, as Psalm 42 does?

2.title: Casting Our Cares on God
2.essay:
“Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Paul does not simply say, “Stop worrying.” He gives an alternative: turn every worry into a prayer.

Everything

Not some things, but everything. Anything big enough to worry about is big enough to pray about. Paul wrote this from prison, facing possible execution, and in the same breath he commanded joy and gentleness. It is not denial of trouble but trust in the God who is near: “The Lord is at hand” (Philippians 4:5). That may mean he is near in presence, or that his return is near. Either way, it is a reason not to be anxious.

We pray because God is sovereign. If he were not in control, prayer would be pointless. Because he rules all things and cares for us, prayer is the most reasonable response to anxiety.

With thanksgiving

Paul adds thanksgiving to prayer. Gratitude shifts our focus from what we lack to what God has given, and thanking him for past faithfulness strengthens our trust for present needs.

The peace that guards

“And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). Paul does not promise that God will give us everything we ask. He promises peace: a peace that does not depend on circumstances and makes no sense to the world. And it guards our hearts like soldiers guarding a city.

Cast them on him

“Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:6–7). Casting is a deliberate act, like throwing a heavy load onto someone stronger. And the reason is simple: he cares for you. Peter goes on to watchfulness against the devil and endurance in suffering, and to a promise: “the God of all grace … will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (1 Peter 5:10). Anxiety is met by God’s care and by the hope of his final restoration.

For many people, casting their anxieties on God is not a single act but a daily or even hourly practice. Each time the worry returns, we cast it again. That is not failure; it is faith exercised.

When I am afraid

David wrote Psalm 56 when the Philistines seized him in Gath. “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (Psalm 56:3–4). He does not say he is never afraid. He says that when fear comes, he turns to God. Faith is not the absence of fear but the decision to trust God in the middle of it, and trust in God puts human threats in perspective.

He will sustain you

In Psalm 55 David has been betrayed by a close friend and is overwhelmed. He calls to God “evening and morning and at noon” (Psalm 55:17). Then he urges others: “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved” (Psalm 55:22). God may not remove the burden at once, but he promises to hold us up under it. The one who prayed in distress now encourages others to do the same.

Spread it before the Lord

When King Hezekiah received a threatening letter from the king of Assyria, he went up to the temple “and spread it before the LORD” (2 Kings 19:14). Then he prayed. God answered and delivered Jerusalem. Hezekiah literally laid his anxiety before God.

A man facing redundancy begins writing his worries in a notebook each morning, turning each into a prayer and adding one thing he is thankful for. He still loses his job. But he finds himself surprisingly at peace, and three months later he finds new work. He keeps the notebook as a record of God’s faithfulness.

Take your biggest worry right now and turn it into a specific prayer, with thanksgiving.

For reflection

Why does Paul tell us to pray “with thanksgiving”? What does it mean that God’s peace “guards” your heart and mind? Which anxiety do you need to cast on God today? How could casting your cares on him become a daily habit?

3.title: Learning Contentment
3.essay:
“Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:11–13).

The secret Paul learned

Contentment is not natural. Paul had to learn it. And it did not depend on circumstances: he was content in both plenty and poverty. He was thanking the Philippians for a gift, but making clear that his contentment had never rested on it.

The secret is Christ himself. The famous verse, “I can do all things through him who strengthens me”, is not about achieving our dreams, but about being content in any circumstance through Christ’s strength. When Christ is our treasure, we can be at peace with or without other things.

Paul knew it in practice. Beaten and in stocks in a Philippian prison, he and Silas “were praying and singing hymns to God” at midnight (Acts 16:25). Their circumstances could hardly have been worse, yet they were content enough to sing — and it was to that same church that he later wrote about learning contentment.

Great gain

“But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content” (1 Timothy 6:6–8). Some were treating godliness as a way to get rich. Paul says contentment is the real gain. Life is short, and we leave it with nothing; contentment sees possessions in that light.

And he warns: “But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:9–10). Discontent can lead to debt, dishonesty and destruction, and some have wandered from the faith through it. Contentment protects the soul.

Who we have

“Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you.’ So we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear’” (Hebrews 13:5–6). The reason for contentment is not what we have but who we have. If God is with us, we have everything we need. Contentment rests on a person, not on possessions.

A beautiful inheritance

David sang, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance” (Psalm 16:5–6). God himself is his people’s portion. Because the Lord is at his right hand, he will not be shaken; his heart is glad and his body rests secure. “In your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11). That is the deepest root of contentment.

And believers can be content now partly because they know what is coming. Present lack is temporary; our inheritance is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).

Contentment and providence

Contentment rests on the belief that God governs our circumstances wisely and lovingly. What he has given is not an accident. What he has withheld, he has withheld for good reasons, even when we cannot see them. The Providence of God study explores this further.

Not complacency

Contentment does not mean we never seek to improve our circumstances, pursue goals or work for change. It means our peace does not depend on those things. A content person can still pray for a spouse, look for a better job or seek healing, without being consumed by the longing.

A couple in their thirties feel behind their friends: a smaller house, an older car, fewer holidays. They start naming three things they are grateful for at dinner each night. Over a year they notice that they compare less and enjoy more. Their circumstances have not changed. Their hearts have.

Finish this sentence: “I would be content if only…” What does your answer reveal?

For reflection

Why do you think Paul had to “learn” contentment? What does Philippians 4:13 really mean in its context? How does God’s promise “I will never leave you” make contentment possible? Name at least five things you are grateful for today.

4.title: The Enemies of Contentment
4.essay:
Contentment has enemies. Recognising them helps us fight them.

Covetousness

The tenth commandment says, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17). It is unique among the commandments in addressing desire rather than action, showing that God cares about the heart, not only behaviour; Paul said this was the commandment that convicted him of sin (Romans 7:7). Covetousness is wanting what belongs to someone else, or wanting more than God has given, so much that it rules the heart.

When a man asked Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus refused, and warned, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). Then he told of the rich fool, who planned for himself, built bigger barns and forgot God — and whose soul was required of him that night. What matters is being “rich toward God” (Luke 12:21). Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5), because it treats things as if they could give what only God gives.

King Ahab had a palace and a kingdom, yet he lay on his bed sulking because Naboth would not sell him his vineyard (1 Kings 21:4). His covetousness led to Naboth’s murder. A king with everything was miserable over one small field.

Comparison

Asaph began Psalm 73 with a confession of faith: God is good to Israel. Then he admitted, “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:2–3). Even believers who know the truth can be shaken by comparison. Comparison breeds envy, and envy kills contentment. Social media has made comparison constant: we see the highlights of others’ lives and measure our ordinary days against them. Honesty about envy is the first step to overcoming it.

A woman realises that every time she scrolls through social media she feels dissatisfied with her home, her body and her life. She takes a month’s break, and spends the time reading the Psalms and writing thank-you notes. At the end of the month she is surprised how much more content she feels.

Grumbling

In the wilderness, Israel complained about food, water and leadership, even after seeing God’s miracles. The rabble among them had a strong craving, and soon all the people were weeping for meat: “We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic. But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at” (Numbers 11:5–6). They remembered Egypt’s food as if it had been free, forgot the slavery, and despised God’s daily miracle. Grumbling rewrites the past and blinds us to present grace.

Forgetting God

Moses warned Israel that once they were prosperous in the land, they might forget the Lord and say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17). Prosperity can be as dangerous to contentment as poverty.

The cure

Asaph’s envy was cured when he went into the sanctuary of God; “then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17). He saw that the wicked stand on slippery ground. He saw his own foolishness — “I was like a beast toward you” — and God’s faithfulness: “Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory” (Psalm 73:23–24). Then came his great confession: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26). Contentment returns when God becomes our treasure again.

Thanksgiving is one of the strongest weapons against discontent. It is hard to covet and give thanks at the same time. And eternity puts comparison in its place. Comparing ourselves with others makes sense only if this life is all there is. In the light of eternity, the differences that seem so large now will look very small.

Whom do you most often compare yourself with? What does that comparison do to your heart?

For reflection

Which enemy of contentment is strongest in your life: covetousness, comparison, grumbling or forgetting God? Read Psalm 73: what turned Asaph’s heart around? How does social media affect your contentment, and what boundaries might help? Write a short prayer of thanks for what God has given you.

5.title: Peace in the Storm
5.essay:
A great windstorm arose on the Sea of Galilee. The disciples, experienced fishermen, were terrified, and Jesus was asleep in the stern. They woke him: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38).

Christ in the boat

He rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” — and there was a great calm. Then he asked them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” (Mark 4:39–40). The disciples had assumed he did not care because he was asleep. In fact he was completely in control. And they were filled with a greater fear, the awe of seeing who he was. The storm was real, but so was the presence of Christ in the boat. Knowing who is in the boat changes everything.

Christ does not always calm the storm at once. Sometimes he calms us in the storm. Either way, he is Lord of the wind and the waves.

Perfect peace

“You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock” (Isaiah 26:3–4). Peace comes from where our minds rest. Fixing our thoughts on God, rather than endlessly rehearsing our fears, brings peace, and our peace rests on his unchanging strength.

God our refuge

“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea” (Psalm 46:1–2). The psalm imagines the worst: the earth giving way, mountains falling into the sea, nations raging. Yet there is a river that makes glad the city of God, and he makes wars cease. Into the chaos he speaks: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). In the middle of upheaval, God’s people can be still.

On the night before his planned execution, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains (Acts 12:6). James had already been killed. Yet Peter slept so soundly that the angel had to strike him on the side to wake him. His peace came from trusting God with his life.

Body and soul

God made us whole people, and anxiety often affects, and is affected by, the body. After his great victory on Mount Carmel, Elijah fled in fear and asked to die. God did not rebuke him. He let him sleep, gave him bread and water, let him sleep again and fed him a second time: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). Only then did he speak to him. God cares for his exhausted servants gently, body and soul.

So rest, exercise, healthy eating and time outdoors are not unspiritual. For some, anxiety has medical causes, or is severe enough to need a doctor’s care. Medication, where appropriate, is a legitimate help, not a sign of weak faith. Body and soul both need attention.

Not alone

No one should face severe anxiety alone. Pastors, wise friends and counsellors can help, and sharing burdens is part of Christian love: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2).

A Christian man has struggled with panic attacks for years and has been ashamed to admit it. He finally tells his pastor, who encourages him to see his doctor. With medical help, counselling and a small group who pray for him, his anxiety slowly becomes manageable. He still has hard days, but he knows he is not alone, and that Christ is in the boat.

Peace with God and the peace of God

Believers have peace with God through justification: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). That is permanent. The peace of God, a felt calm in the heart, may come and go. But the first is the foundation of the second. Even on anxious days, our peace with God is secure.

And anxious feelings do not necessarily mean weak faith. Faith often acts while feelings lag behind. Trusting God in the middle of anxiety is real faith.

His peace

Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27). His peace is a gift now, and it will be complete when he returns and every cause of fear is removed.

Is there someone you could talk to about your anxieties, rather than carrying them alone?

For reflection

Read Mark 4:35–41: what does it teach you about Christ’s presence in your storms? What does it mean for your mind to be “stayed” on God? How does God’s care for Elijah show that body and soul both matter? Who could you share your anxieties with this week?
